strengths: The paper proposes a coherent coordinate-free GUI grounding approach that supervises intrinsic MLLM attention maps rather than adding a separate grounding head or generating coordinates as text. The anchor-token formulation and visual-sink query based head weighting are technically plausible and fit the stated motivation.

Empirical results are strong for a 3B model, especially on ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G. The paper compares against general MLLMs, SFT GUI models, and RL-tuned GUI models, and reports clear gains over same-scale Qwen2.5-VL based baselines.

The ablation study is useful: it separates vanilla attention grounding, anchor-based simplified grounding, several head-weighting strategies, visual-sink token choices, soft weighting, and weighted patch labels. This supports the claim that the improvements are not due to a single incidental implementation choice.

The two-step crop/zoom inference is simple and practically relevant for high-resolution GUIs, and the paper provides an analysis of recovered versus lost predictions rather than only reporting the final score.
The contribution is well aligned with the Algorithms/General category: it introduces a modeling/training method and evaluates it on standard GUI grounding benchmarks with appropriate metrics.
weaknesses: The strongest reported ScreenSpot-Pro result relies on a two-pass zoom-in procedure, but this is not applied to competing baselines. Since the method roughly doubles inference cost and changes the test-time protocol, the comparison between one-step baselines and GUI-AIMA + zoom-in is not fully controlled.

The paper repeatedly emphasizes efficiency and data efficiency, but the evidence is incomplete. It reports fewer screenshots than some baselines, yet does not provide training time, inference latency, memory, FLOPs, or fair re-training comparisons under matched data and compute budgets.

Several baseline numbers are copied from original papers, with missing entries and potentially different training data, preprocessing, prompts, image resolutions, and inference settings. This weakens the strength of the ranking claims, especially when margins are moderate on ScreenSpot-v2 and OSWorld-G.

The method depends on attention behavior in Qwen2.5-VL and on a newly introduced anchor token, but the paper gives limited analysis of robustness across backbones, model scales, image tokenization schemes, or instruction styles. It is therefore unclear how general the claimed intrinsic attention alignment is beyond the chosen 3B backbone.

The visual-sink query token analysis is relatively shallow. The explanation often asserts that hidden-state similarity identifies semantic visual-sink tokens, but the evidence is mostly small qualitative plots and downstream ablations; there is little diagnostic analysis of what tokens are selected across datasets or failure cases.

Reproducibility is not yet convincing. The project page is blank in the abstract, and important implementation details such as exact prompt format, coordinate-to-patch conversion edge cases, crop selection behavior, benchmark preprocessing, and whether all datasets are filtered for benchmark overlap are insufficiently specified.

The paper would benefit from stronger limitation and failure analysis. It discusses offset errors helped by zoom-in, but gives less attention to cases where patch-level grounding fails semantically, where the correct element is very small, partially occluded, repeated, or requires contextual reasoning outside the visible crop.

Writing and presentation need polishing. There are grammar issues, typos, dense equations with inconsistent notation, and some tables are hard to read in extracted form. These do not invalidate the work, but they make the technical argument less crisp.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: GUI grounding for computer-use agents, especially under high-resolution and visually dense interfaces.

The core idea of supervising intrinsic MLLM attention with patch-wise labels is plausible and attractive because it avoids adding a separate grounding head, and the anchor-token formulation is a reasonable simplification of prior attention-grounding approaches.

The reported results are strong for a 3B model, particularly on ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G, and the paper includes useful ablations for anchor-based aggregation, visual-sink query token selection, weighted patch labels, and zoom-in inference.
The method is relatively simple to implement on top of Qwen2.5-VL and appears data-efficient compared with many GUI-specialized SFT baselines.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is not fully convincing. Many baseline numbers are taken from original papers, some entries are unreported, and it is unclear whether all methods use identical evaluation protocols, image resolutions, prompt formats, preprocessing, and test-time procedures. This is especially problematic because small changes in GUI grounding evaluation can materially affect accuracy.

The strongest headline result on ScreenSpot-Pro relies on the two-step zoom-in procedure, but comparable test-time refinement is not applied to baselines. This makes the main SOTA claim difficult to interpret; without zoom-in, GUI-AIMA is much less dominant and is only modestly ahead of some same-scale baselines.

The novelty is incremental relative to TAG/attention grounding and GUI-Actor-style coordinate-free grounding. The anchor token, head weighting via visual-sink tokens, and soft patch labels are sensible engineering choices, but the paper does not establish a deeper algorithmic advance beyond this combination.

Several methodological details are under-specified for reproducibility, including exact prompt/grounding format, how patch centers are converted back to click points, crop selection at image boundaries, whether screenshots are resized consistently across datasets, and how the authors generated the missing GUI-G2-3B baseline result.

The training data mixture raises possible contamination or overlap concerns with GUI benchmarks, but the paper does not provide a rigorous dataset overlap audit. Since the method is trained on large GUI datasets including samples from recent GUI-agent sources, this is important for evaluating generalization claims.

The analysis of visual-sink query tokens is not sufficiently rigorous. The evidence mostly consists of ablations and qualitative token-correlation plots, but the proposed interpretation of attention heads and hidden-state similarity is not strongly validated.

The paper overstates some claims, such as 'exceptional data efficiency' and broad generalization, given that training still uses 259k instructions and around 85k screenshots, and comparisons to much larger systems are confounded by different data, protocols, and test-time inference.

Clarity is uneven: there are typos and grammatical issues, the project page field is blank, some equations/normalizations are confusingly described, and the relationship between coordinate-free patch prediction and final coordinate/click evaluation could be explained more precisely.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful Algorithms/General contribution for GUI grounding: aligning intrinsic MLLM self-attention with patch-wise grounding labels via an anchor token, visual-sink query-token based head weighting, and overlap/center-aware patch labels. The approach is conceptually appealing because it avoids coordinate-token generation and avoids adding a separate grounding head.

Empirical results are strong for a 3B model. GUI-AIMA substantially improves over Qwen2.5-VL-3B and same-scale GUI grounding methods on ScreenSpot-Pro, is competitive on ScreenSpot-v2, and improves OSWorld-G; the zoom-in variant is especially strong on high-resolution settings.

The ablation study is meaningful. It isolates vanilla attention grounding, simplified anchor attention, several head-weighting variants, visual-sink token choices, patch-label weighting, and training convergence, giving a convincing case that the main components contribute.

The method has practical appeal: one-stage fine-tuning on a relatively modest dataset, no extra task-specific grounding module, and a plug-and-play zoom-in inference procedure that fits the coordinate-free formulation.
The paper is generally well organized and positions itself clearly relative to coordinate-based GUI grounding, TAG, and GUI-Actor.
weaknesses: Some experimental comparisons are not fully controlled. Many baseline numbers are taken from original papers, and training data, preprocessing, resolution, prompt format, and test-time settings may differ. This weakens the strength of claims such as outperforming larger models, even though the reported results are promising.

The two-step zoom-in inference is effective but introduces additional test-time computation and a somewhat hand-designed crop/zoom policy. The paper would benefit from clearer runtime/latency reporting and fair comparison to other methods with similar crop or test-time refinement.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places. The project link appears blank in the abstract, code/model release is not clearly specified, and important implementation details such as exact formatting, patch mapping, inference aggregation, and benchmark preprocessing are not sufficiently explicit for easy reproduction.

The paper’s explanation of visual-sink query tokens is plausible but still somewhat heuristic. The analysis supports the design empirically, but the mechanism is not deeply validated beyond limited examples and ablations.

The method remains specialized to single-region GUI grounding and does not evaluate downstream GUI-agent task success. The paper claims relevance to computer-use agents, but evidence is mostly point-grounding accuracy rather than end-to-end action performance.
Writing quality is understandable but contains several grammatical issues and minor terminology inconsistencies, which occasionally make the technical presentation harder to follow.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem for computer-use agents: GUI grounding from screenshots. The proposed contribution type is best treated as Algorithms/General, and the paper makes a coherent algorithmic case for replacing coordinate-token generation with supervised intrinsic attention over visual patches.

The method is technically plausible and relatively elegant: the anchor token provides a simple way to aggregate query-conditioned visual attention, visual-sink query tokens give an adaptive head-weighting mechanism, and the patch-wise label plus zoom-in inference are well matched to GUI localization.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2, and ScreenSpot-v1 in the appendix. Results are strong for a 3B model, especially on ScreenSpot-Pro with zoom-in, ScreenSpot-v2, and OSWorld-G.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: anchor-based simplified attention improves over vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor under the same 45k setting; visual-sink token weighting and weighted patch labels each add measurable gains; additional appendix ablations on a larger training set broadly agree.

The paper makes a credible data-efficiency argument relative to GUI-Actor and some large-scale baselines, and the training/inference-time discussion helps clarify the practical cost of extracting attention maps.
weaknesses: Some comparisons are difficult to interpret because training data and evaluation domains differ substantially across methods. GUI-AIMA-3B adds GroundCUA data and UI-Vision is explicitly in-domain; several baselines use very different data scales or unavailable details. The paper reports strong numbers, but the fairness of the headline comparisons is not always cleanly separated from data effects.

The novelty is incremental relative to TAG and GUI-Actor. The anchor-token aggregation and visual-sink head weighting are sensible, but the core idea of using attention for coordinate-free GUI grounding is already established. The paper would be stronger with deeper analysis showing why the learned attention remains robust beyond benchmark distributions.

The two-step zoom-in procedure contributes large gains on ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G, but its implementation details are under-specified: crop selection, boundary handling, final coordinate conversion, and failure cases need clearer description. It is also not fully disentangled from the core training contribution in the main results.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The project page field is blank, and important details such as exact data preprocessing, loss balancing with next-token prediction, click-center derivation from patch distributions, and benchmark-specific inference settings are not fully specified in the main paper.

The method remains limited by patch resolution and by needing ground-truth boxes converted to patch labels, so the claim of being coordinate-free should be interpreted narrowly: it avoids coordinate-token generation, but still depends on spatial labels and ultimately produces point clicks. The paper could be clearer about this distinction.

Some presentation issues reduce polish and confidence, including malformed symbols around the zoom-in notation, occasional grammar problems, dense tables with hard-to-read formatting, and a few claims that overstate results where performance is competitive rather than clearly superior.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: GUI grounding for computer-use agents, especially under high-resolution desktop interfaces where coordinate-token generation is brittle.

The proposed attention-supervision framing is conceptually clean: using an anchor token to aggregate query-conditioned visual attention and weighting heads via visual-sink query tokens is a plausible way to exploit existing MLLM attention without adding a separate grounding head.

The empirical coverage is broad, including ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, and MMBench-GUI-L2, with ablations for the anchor formulation, head weighting, patch-wise labels, and zoom-in inference.
The method appears data-efficient relative to some large GUI grounding systems, and the two-step zoom-in procedure gives substantial gains on high-resolution benchmarks.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited and somewhat incremental relative to TAG, GUI-Actor, SE-GUI, and other recent coordinate-free or attention-based GUI grounding work. The paper combines an anchor token, attention supervision, head weighting, patch labels, and zoom-in inference, but the conceptual leap over prior attention-grounding methods is not fully convincing.

The main performance claims are difficult to assess fairly because comparisons use heterogeneous training data, model scales, benchmark overlap conditions, and results copied from prior papers. Some baselines are not rerun under the same data and inference protocol, and the strongest reported gains often include the proposed two-step zoom-in procedure without applying comparable test-time refinement to competing methods.

Several claims are overstated. For example, the paper presents state-of-the-art or highly competitive results, but GUI-AIMA is not consistently best: on UI-Vision it trails GroundNext-3B RL, and on MMBench-GUI-L2 it trails larger Holo2 models. On ScreenSpot-v2, gains over strong Qwen3 and GUI-Actor baselines are small or depend on different setups.

The precise inference mechanism from patch-level attention to final click coordinates is under-specified. The paper says the model first identifies relevant patches and then determines the exact click location, but the actual conversion from attention distribution to click point, handling of multiple positive patches, and behavior for small UI elements are not described in enough detail for confident reproduction.

The ablations do not fully isolate the sources of improvement in the final system. The 45k ablation setting shows moderate gains, while the headline numbers combine larger/different data and zoom-in. It remains unclear how much comes from the proposed attention alignment versus extra desktop-domain data, patch labeling borrowed from GUI-G2, and the second inference pass.

The visual-sink query-token mechanism is weakly justified. The selected top tokens are often stopwords or punctuation, and the explanation that these are functional cross-modal proxies is plausible but not deeply validated. The supporting analysis is mostly correlational and does not establish why this weighting should generalize.

Reproducibility is incomplete: training data mixtures are described only at a high level, baseline result sourcing is uneven, project page is blank in the abstract, and implementation details such as attention extraction, normalization, crop boundary handling, and final coordinate decoding need more specificity.

The writing has a number of clarity and polish issues, including formatting artifacts, awkward phrasing, duplicated references, and occasional imprecision. These do not alone invalidate the work, but they reinforce the impression that the scientific case is not yet carefully packaged.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem for GUI agents: grounding natural-language instructions to screen regions without relying on coordinate-token generation. The proposed framing of GUI grounding as supervised intrinsic attention alignment is well motivated and practically relevant.

The main technical idea is clean: an appended anchor token aggregates query context under causal attention, while visual-sink query tokens provide an adaptive way to weight grounding-relevant attention heads. This gives a coordinate-free method without extra grounding heads or a separate warm-up module.

The empirical results are strong for a 3B model. GUI-AIMA reports competitive or state-of-the-art performance among similarly sized models on ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, MMBench-GUI-L2, and UI-Vision, with especially convincing gains on high-resolution desktop benchmarks when using the zoom-in stage.

The ablation study is substantial. The paper isolates vanilla attention grounding, anchor-based simplification, head-weighting variants, visual-sink token selection, patch-wise labeling, and zoom-in inference, making the contribution of each component fairly easy to assess.

The method appears data- and training-efficient relative to GUI-Actor and large-scale coordinate-based systems: it avoids extra modules, uses one-stage fine-tuning, and reports lower training GPU-hours while maintaining similar inference cost.

The coordinate-free formulation naturally supports the crop-and-zoom inference procedure, which is a useful practical advantage for high-resolution GUI grounding and is backed by an offset-error analysis.
weaknesses: Some comparisons are difficult to interpret cleanly because training data differs substantially across methods. GUI-AIMA-3B adds GroundCUA data and UI-Vision is explicitly in-domain for both GUI-AIMA-3B and GroundNext, so the strongest claims about architectural superiority over data scale should be phrased more cautiously.

The visual-sink query token mechanism is empirically useful but conceptually under-explained. The top selected tokens are often function words, punctuation, or newline-like tokens, so the causal story that these tokens are reliable proxies for cross-modal grounding remains somewhat heuristic despite the ablations.

The method depends on access to internal attention maps and on modifying the input/token format with anchor tokens, which may limit portability to closed MLLMs or architectures where attention extraction is expensive or unavailable. This limitation is not discussed in depth.

The zoom-in stage improves results substantially but adds a second forward pass and uses fixed crop/zoom hyperparameters. The paper reports that the zoom factor is not highly sensitive, but more analysis of failure modes, latency tradeoffs, and cases where the second pass loses originally correct predictions would strengthen the practical case.

The evaluation is still primarily static center-point grounding. There is limited evidence that the improved grounding translates into better end-to-end GUI agent task completion, multi-step interaction, or robustness under dynamic UI changes.

Reproducibility is only partially supported in the manuscript. The project page placeholder appears empty, code release is unclear, and several baseline numbers are taken from different papers or external reports; this makes independent verification of the full comparison harder.

The writing is generally understandable but has polish issues, including typos, awkward phrasing, and stray symbols in section text. These do not undermine the technical case, but they should be cleaned up for publication.
